411.quote_or_event: “Four things of paramount value are difficult to obtain here by a living being: human birth, instruction in the Law, belief in it, and energy in self-control.”
411.explanation: Jainism lists hearing the Law (Prakrit sui, Sanskrit sruti, i.e. hearing) among the four rarest and most valuable things a soul can gain. Jacobi translates it as 'instruction in the Law'.
411.tie_back: Valluvar calls the wealth of the ear foremost among all kinds of wealth. The Uttaradhyayana likewise ranks hearing the Law among the few gifts of 'paramount value'.
411.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 3.1 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
411._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The identification of 'instruction in the Law' with hearing follows the lecture's own verses 8-11 ('having heard the Law'). This is a strong fit, though the Jain text lists hearing as one of four treasures rather than the single foremost one.

412.quote_or_event: “In the first Paurushî he should study, in the second he should meditate, in the third he should go on his begging-tour, and in the fourth he should study again.”
412.explanation: The Jain monk's daily routine puts study first. Looking for food comes only in the third quarter of the day, after study and meditation, and the fourth quarter is again for study.
412.tie_back: The Kural tells us to give the stomach a little only when there is no food for the ear. The Jain monk's day, in which the alms round waits until study and meditation are done, puts the same order into practice.
412.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 26.12 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
412._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. The ordering of study before food matches well, but this is a monastic timetable rather than a saying about hearing as such.

413.quote_or_event: “As Sakra the thousand-eyed, the wielder of the thunderbolt, the fortress-destroyer, the king of gods, (has no equal), neither has a very learned monk.”
413.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana's lecture on the very learned (bahussuya, literally 'one who has heard much') ranks such a monk as without equal, like Indra among the gods.
413.tie_back: Valluvar says those rich in learning gained by hearing are equal on earth to the gods. The Jain text matches the 'much-heard' monk with the king of the gods.
413.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.23 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
413._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com. Close on comparing the learned with gods. In Jainism, however, gods are embodied beings still in samsara and are not fed by sacrificial oblations, so the kural's sacrificial image has no Jain counterpart.

414.quote_or_event: Rauhineya, a thief, had been told by his dying father never to listen to Mahavira. Passing the assembly with his ears covered, he trod on a thorn, took a hand away to pull it out, and briefly heard Mahavira describing the gods: their feet do not touch the ground, their eyes do not blink, they do not sweat, and their garlands do not wither. Later, minister Abhayakumara tried to trick him into confessing by staging a fake heaven. The few words Rauhineya had overheard let him see through the trap, and he went on to become Mahavira's disciple.
414.explanation: In this Jain story a few words, heard unwillingly by an unlettered man, saved him in his worst crisis and changed his life.
414.tie_back: Valluvar urges even someone who has never studied to listen, because what he hears will be a staff to lean on in adversity. Rauhineya's few overheard words served him in exactly that way.
414.source: Hemacandra, Trisastisalakapurusacaritra, Parva X, ch. 11, 'Story of Rauhineya' (tr. Helen M. Johnson, GOS; wisdomlib.org)
414._accuracy_note: Paraphrased. A search confirmed that wisdomlib.org's Johnson translation has this section (Parva X, ch. XI), but the page returned a server error, so the details were checked against several Jain retellings. Very close fit to listening as a support in adversity.

415.quote_or_event: “A needle with a thread (in it) does not get lost even when it falls in a heap of rubbish, so a person endowed with scriptureal knowledge does not lose his self, even if involved in transmigratory cycle.”
415.explanation: The Saman Suttam's verses on right knowledge compare scriptural knowledge to the thread that keeps a needle from being lost. Through it the soul keeps hold of itself even in the confusion of samsara.
415.tie_back: Valluvar compares the words of the virtuous to a staff for someone walking on slippery ground. The Jain image of the threaded needle likewise presents received teaching as what keeps a person from being lost amid danger.
415.source: Saman Suttam v. 248 (Samyagjnanasutra) (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)
415._accuracy_note: Checked word for word (including the source's spelling 'scriptureal') on the jainworld.com Saman Suttam text. The image differs (needle and thread versus walking staff), but the function, received teaching that keeps one safe, is the same.

416.quote_or_event: “After listening to scriptures, a person comes to know what is good and what is sinful, having thus known through listening one ought to perform what leads to welfare.”
416.explanation: This Jain verse (Prakrit 'socca janai kallanam') makes hearing the source of moral knowledge. From listening one learns good and evil and then acts for one's welfare.
416.tie_back: Valluvar urges us to listen to what is good, however little, because it leads to greatness. The Jain verse likewise traces right action and welfare back to hearing.
416.source: Saman Suttam v. 245 (Samyagjnanasutra); the Prakrit is from the Dasavaikalika Sutra 4 (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)
416._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on the jainworld.com Saman Suttam text. Strong on hearing as the root of good, but the verse lacks the kural's stress on how even a little hearing is enough. The Dasavaikalika origin is the standard attribution and was not checked separately.

417.quote_or_event: “Again, under the influence of his (scriptural) knowledge, he becomes firm in his faith, meditation, observance of vows and self-restraint, and lives a life of purity throughout his lifetime without any wavering.”
417.explanation: In the Jain view, knowledge received from scripture gives steadiness, so a person stays firm in faith and conduct without wavering.
417.tie_back: Valluvar says those who have searched deeply and heard much will not speak foolishly even when they have misunderstood something. The Jain verse likewise credits well-absorbed teaching with keeping a person steady.
417.source: Saman Suttam v. 246 (Samyagjnanasutra) (English tr. as published on jainworld.com)
417._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on the jainworld.com Saman Suttam text. Reasonable but partial fit: it speaks of steadiness in conduct, not of avoiding foolish speech after a mistake.

418.quote_or_event: “Though men destitute of rectitude listen to those who are destitute of envy, when they declare the way of virtue, yet they give no heed, just as the chakler's dog, which seizes and devours leather, knows not how to appreciate the taste of rice and milk.”
418.explanation: The Naladiyar describes people who physically hear the teaching of virtue yet take none of it in, like a dog used to leather that cannot taste good food.
418.tie_back: Valluvar says ears never pierced by instruction are as good as deaf, even though they hear sounds. The Naladiyar shows the same kind of hearing, where words arrive and nothing enters.
418.source: Naladiyar, ch. 33 'Defective knowledge', stanza 2 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
418._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Close fit on hearing without taking anything in. This is a Tamil Jain text, not canonical scripture.

419.quote_or_event: “But for the following fifteen good qualities he is called well-behaved: if he is always humble, steady, free from deceit and curiosity; if he abuses nobody; … if he listens to friendly advice; if he is not proud of his learning; … if he is enlightened, polite, decent, and quiet: then he is called well-behaved.”
419.explanation: The lecture on the very learned pairs real learning with humility, courtesy and restrained speech. It lists listening to advice, abusing no one, and being polite and quiet among the marks of the well-trained monk.
419.tie_back: Valluvar says that without refined learning gained by hearing it is hard to have humble, courteous speech. The Uttaradhyayana likewise sets humility, polite speech and readiness to listen among the qualities that come with learning.
419.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 11.10–13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
419._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on sacred-texts.com; the ellipses mark omitted items from the list. A good thematic fit, but the verse lists virtues and does not say that learning produces courteous speech.

420.quote_or_event: “Although they see by numerous examples the way by which their precious life may depart in the twinkling of an eye, yet they do not good even to the extent of a grain of millet. What does it matter whether such stupid, shameless (persons) live, or whether they die?”
420.explanation: The Naladiyar's chapter on defective knowledge dismisses people who learn nothing from what they see and do no good. It asks whether it matters at all if such people live or die.
420.tie_back: Valluvar asks what it matters whether people who know only the tastes of the mouth, not of the ear, live or die. The Naladiyar asks the same question, almost word for word, about the stupid who take in nothing.
420.source: Naladiyar, ch. 33 'Defective knowledge', stanza 3 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
420._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. The closing question is nearly identical to the kural's, but the Naladiyar's target is people who ignore mortality, not people who prefer the palate to the ear. This is a Tamil Jain text.
